To view a copy of this license, visit http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ We recently reported that circulating apolipoprotein AII (apoAII) isoforms apoAII-ATQ/AT (C-terminal truncations of the apoAII homo-dimer) decline significantly in pancreatic cancer and thus might serve as plasma biomarkers for the early detection of this disease. We report here the development of novel enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) for measurement of apoAII-ATQ/AT and their clinical applicability for early detection of pancreatic cancer. Plasma and serum concentrations of apoAII-ATQ/AT were measured in three independent cohorts, which comprised healthy control subjects and patients with pancreatic cancer and gastroenterologic diseases (n = 1156). These cohorts included 151 cases of stage I/II pancreatic cancer. ApoAII-ATQ/AT not only distinguished the early stages of pancreatic cancer from healthy controls but also identified patients at high risk for pancreatic malignancy. AUC values of apoAII-ATQ/AT to detect early stage pancreatic cancer were higher than those of CA19–9 in all independent cohorts. ApoAII-ATQ/AT is a potential biomarker for screening patients for the early stage of pancreatic cancer and identifying patients at risk for pancreatic malignancy (161 words). Pancreatic cancer is one of the most lethal solid malignant tumors. To decrease the mortality of pancreatic cancer, efficient screening methods that will enable detection of the early stage of the disease and the identification of the precancerous lesions that are thought to be risk factors for pancreatic malignancy are needed 1 2 . Plasma/serum biomarkers for the early detection of pancreatic cancer would be useful clinical tools for screening patients in order to identify those who should undergo a second screening using stricter diagnostic modalities that can detect pancreatic dysfunction before imaging 3 . We recently reported the results of a mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomic analysis, which showed that the levels of five circulating isoforms of apolipoprotein-AII (apoAII), including two novel isoforms, are significantly different in the plasma of patients with invasive ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreas (IDACP) relative to healthy controls 4 5 . The five circulating apoAII-isoforms are characterized by the truncation of varying numbers of amino acids from the C-terminus of the apoAII homo-dimer. The isoforms were designated apoAII-ATQ/ATQ (apoAII-1, 17,380 Da) (the descriptions of -ATQ/ATQ etc. showed that each had the C-terminal sequence of an apo-AII isoform), apoAII-ATQ/AT (apoAII-2, 17,252 Da), apoAII-AT/AT (apoAII-3, 17,124 Da), apoAII-AT/A (apoAII-4, 17,023 Da), and apoAII-A/A (apoAII-5, 16,922 Da) ( Supplemental Figure 1 ) 5 . The circulating isoforms could be distinguished according to differences in molecular weight as determined by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-mass spectrometry (MALDI-MS) 5 . We previously reported the development of a novel and sophisticated MALDI-MS method for the semi-quantitative measurement of the levels of apoAII-isoforms in plasma. This MALDI-MS method was used to analyze more than 1,300 plasma/serum samples collected from patients at multiple medical institutions in Japan and Germany, in a previous study 5 . These analyses showed a statistically significant decrease in the level of apoAII-ATQ/AT in plasma and serum of IDACP patients compared with healthy controls from four independent cohorts 5 . These results suggested that apoAII-ATQ/AT would be good candidate plasma biomarkers for use in diagnosing early stage pancreatic cancer 5 6 , unlike other isoforms such as apoAII-ATQ/ATQ, -AT/AT, AT/A and A/A 5 . However, several factors impeded the clinical application of our MALDI-MS–based method for the measurement of apoAII-ATQ/AT. In this study, we developed novel sandwich ELISAs for the measurement of apoAII-isoforms in clinical samples. Our sandwich ELISAs provide for robust and rapid analysis of apoAII-isoforms. We evaluated the assays by measuring the plasma levels of apoAII-isoforms in samples from patients with pancreatic cancer and pancreatic disorders, including precancerous lesions and various malignant diseases of other organs, and we then compared the results with those of healthy controls. The Early Detection Research Network (EDRN), an initiative of the National Cancer Institute (NCI), is a consortium of institutions with the goal of accelerating the translation of biomarker information into clinical applications for the early detection of cancer ( http://edrn.nci.nih.gov ). The objectives of the EDRN include the development and testing of promising biomarkers or technologies for early detection of cancer and the evaluation of promising, analytically proven biomarkers or technologies. The EDRN has reference sets available for validating promising biomarkers for the early detection of cancer. The Japanese team applied for and received the pancreatic cancer reference set to validate the apoAII-isoforms biomarker for early detection of this cancer.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Pancreatic cancer, particularly Invasive Ductal Adenocarcinoma of the Pancreas (IDACP), and other related pancreatic and gastroenterologic disorders.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: The biomarker, apolipoprotein AII (apoAII) isoforms (specifically C-terminal truncations of the apoAII homo-dimer like apoAII-ATQ/AT), exhibits significantly altered levels in patients with invasive ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreas (IDACP) compared to healthy controls. These alterations manifest as unique distributions of circulating apoAII-isoform homo-dimers, categorized into hypo-processing (e.g., predominant apoAII-ATQ/ATQ) or hyper-processing (e.g., predominant apoAII-AT/AT, -AT/A, or -A/A). Hypo-processing may indicate a pancreatic inability to synthesize exopeptidases, while hyper-processing might result from increased activity of specific exopeptidases (such as carboxypeptidase A) released from the pancreas. The observed decrease in apoAII-ATQ/AT levels in IDACP is attributed to these processing imbalances, potentially involving reductions in apoAII-AT and -ATQ or an increase in apoAII-ATQ coupled with a decrease in apoAII-AT.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The apoAII-ATQ/AT biomarker consistently shows significantly lower concentrations in plasma samples from IDACP patients (average 36.6 µg/ml) compared to healthy controls (average 66.7 µg/ml) across all stages (I-IV), with distinct differences noted even in early stages (I and II). The ELISA for apoAII-ATQ/AT demonstrates excellent discrimination for early-stage (I/II) IDACP, achieving AUC values greater than 0.9 in Japanese cohorts, and its AUC values for stage-I IDACP surpassed those of CA19-9 and DUPAN-2. While CA19-9 levels increase with pancreatic cancer progression (e.g., significant increases in stages IA/IB/IIA and IIB), the combination of CA19-9 and apoAII-ATQ/AT yields a statistically significant improvement in AUC (0.0978, 95% CI 0.040–0.169) for early-stage detection, offering high sensitivity (95.4%) and specificity (98.3%) for detecting stage-I and stage-II IDACP. Staging was conducted using UICC and AJCC (7th ed.) guidelines.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The developed sandwich ELISAs for apoAII-ATQ and apoAII-AT demonstrate high analytical specificity, with no cross-reactivity. Clinically, apoAII-ATQ/AT effectively distinguishes early-stage pancreatic cancer and patients at high risk for pancreatic malignancy from healthy controls, showing higher AUC values than CA19-9 for early detection. The biomarker's levels are significantly lower in IDACP across all stages. While apoAII-ATQ/AT levels also decrease in various other gastroenterologic diseases (including pancreatic diseases other than IDACP, cholangiocarcinoma, duodenal carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, esophageal, gastric, and colorectal cancers), the most pronounced decreases in apoAII-ATQ or -AT are observed in IDACP and pancreatic diseases. This suggests that a two-dimensional analysis of apoAII-ATQ and -AT levels might help discriminate pancreatic diseases from other conditions. Importantly, apoAII-isoform levels are not significantly correlated with total bilirubin, indicating they are not confounded by acute biliary obstruction. However, apoAII-isoforms alone cannot differentiate IDACP from other specific pancreatic diseases such as endocrine tumors, IPMN, MCN, SCN, and chronic pancreatitis. The EDRN reference set facilitated unbiased evaluation and comparison of biomarker specificity.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Healthy control subjects, patients with invasive ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreas (IDACP) across all stages (I-IV), patients with other pancreatic diseases (e.g., endocrine neoplasms, intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs), mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs), serous cystic neoplasms (SCNs), chronic pancreatitis, acute benign biliary obstruction), patients at high risk for pancreatic malignancy, and patients with other gastroenterologic diseases (e.g., cholangiocarcinoma, duodenal carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, esophageal carcinoma, gastric carcinoma, colorectal carcinoma). Specific cohorts included Japanese cohorts and the NCI-EDRN pancreatic cancer reference set.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: The apoAII-isoform ELISAs, specifically for apoAII-ATQ/AT, offer significant diagnostic utility for the early detection of pancreatic cancer, particularly invasive ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreas (IDACP), aiming to decrease its high mortality. This biomarker enables the identification of early-stage disease (Stage I/II) and individuals at high risk for pancreatic malignancy, serving as a valuable tool for initial screening before more stringent diagnostic modalities. ApoAII-ATQ/AT demonstrates superior diagnostic accuracy (AUC) compared to existing markers like CA19-9 and DUPAN-2 in early stages. Furthermore, a combination assay utilizing apoAII-ATQ/AT and CA19-9 significantly enhances diagnostic accuracy, providing high sensitivity and specificity for IDACP, including its early stages, and effectively compensates for the limitations of CA19-9 in early diagnosis or in Lewis antigen-negative patients.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: The apoAII-ATQ/AT biomarker provides robust diagnostic utility for the early detection of pancreatic cancer, specifically IDACP, and is effective for risk stratification by identifying individuals at high risk for pancreatic malignancy. It represents an improved diagnostic tool for enhanced early detection and risk assessment.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: Novel, robust, and rapid enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) have been developed for apoAII-isoforms (apoAII-ATQ and apoAII-AT), demonstrating high specificity, no cross-reactivity, and good correlation with mass spectrometry (MS) results (CC=0.831 for apoAII-AT, CC=0.862 for apoAII-ATQ, and CC=0.824 for calculated apoAII-ATQ/AT). These ELISAs were clinically validated across three independent cohorts (n=1156, including 151 stage I/II pancreatic cancer cases), showing superior performance (higher AUCs) compared to CA19-9 and DUPAN-2 for early pancreatic cancer detection and identifying at-risk patients. A blind validation using the NCI-EDRN pancreatic reference set confirmed significant changes and good AUCs, with apoAII-ATQ/AT outperforming CA19-9 for early-stage cancer. The linear combination of log-transformed CA19-9 and apoAII-ATQ/AT further enhances diagnostic reliability. While ELISA-based measurements offer standardized and lower-error quantification than MS, recognizing that ELISA-ApoAII-ATQ and ELISA-ApoAII-AT act as surrogate biomarkers for apoAII-ATQ/ATQ and apoAII-AT/AT respectively, and the calculated apoAII-ATQ/AT value is a good surrogate for its MS quantification, despite some variability across cohorts (Japanese vs. EDRN, potentially due to sample type or racial differences) and existing overlaps between disease groups.
recommended_alternatives: A combination assay utilizing CA19-9 and apoAII-ATQ/AT (using a linear logistic regression model) is strongly recommended for enhanced early detection of stage-I and stage-II IDACP, offering improved sensitivity (95.4%) and specificity (98.3%) and compensating for CA19-9's limitations.
Specific isoforms of apoAII (measured by ELISA) are recommended over measuring the whole amount of apoAII for pancreatic cancer screening.
Further comparisons and combined use of different candidate biomarkers are suggested.
